China Tightens Export Controls on Drone Parts, Eases Curbs on Farm Models

China will tighten export controls on key drone components while easing restrictions on some agricultural drones, under changes taking effect Nov. 18.
The measures add certain brushless motors, electronic speed controllers and carbon fiber blades to China’s dual-use export control list. They also raise the capacity threshold for controlled drone-mounted aerosol dispensers, reducing licensing requirements for some agricultural models.

articles.title: China to Introduce Export Controls on TBMs, other Cutting Edge Technologies, may Hit India - Revoi.in
articles.summary: China to Introduce Export Controls on TBMs, other Cutting Edge Technologies, may Hit India  Revoi.in
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI, Oct 19: China on Monday said it would introduce export controls on tunnel-boring machines “to better safeguard national security and interests,” starting November 18.
India has already been facing difficulties in customs clearance and delays in importing TBMs from China for several critical infrastructure projects. The latest announcement comes days after Beijing announced a plan to impose sweeping export controls on 40 cutting-edge technologies including those for certain advanced solar manufacturing and some AI platforms.
In an announcement on Monday, the Chinese Commerce Ministry said it was “introducing export controls on tunnel-boring machines and related items and optimising and adjusting export-control measures for certain dredgers and related items.” The measures will take effect on November 18.
The Ministry said prior to the announcement, China had “notified the relevant countries and regions with which it has established export-control dialogue mechanisms.” “The items covered by these measures have clear dual-use (civilian and military) characteristics,” the announcement said. “The measures are intended to better safeguard national security and interests, while also enabling China to better fulfil its international obligations, including those related to non-proliferation.”
India has previously raised with China the delays in customs clearance for imports of TBMs, which are used in India for several critical projects including the construction of metro rail networks in cities, railway corridors and key tunnelling projects including in border areas.
India is dependent on imports for the machines. Difficulties in imports from China started in 2024. In October of that year, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal had publicly raised the issue with visiting German Vice Chancellor Robert Habeck, pointing out that China was blocking the export of TBMs made by a German company in China.
On Monday, China also announced export control measures related to certain types of drones. The controlled items include “autopilots specially designed for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) with a maximum endurance of three hours or more; certain engines specially designed for UAVs or unmanned airships; and UAVs with a range of 300 kilometres or more” among other items.
The latest announcements followed Beijing on October 16 unveiling a sweeping draft plan to restrict exports of more than 40 cutting-edge technologies, including solar manufacturing technologies, some AI models, and certain biotech platforms.
A number of technologies related to the manufacture of solar cells have been listed for either a complete export ban or restricted exports. While the draft plan does not restrict most solar exports, the new controls on next-generation solar manufacturing technologies could impact efforts by countries including India to reduce dependence on China as they look to move up the solar manufacturing chain.
(Manas Dasgupta)

articles.title: What China's Proposed Solar Technology Export Controls Mean for the Global Energy Transition - Construction Review
articles.summary: What China's Proposed Solar Technology Export Controls Mean for the Global Energy Transition  Construction Review
articles.full_text:
China’s proposal for export controls on key solar manufacturing technologies could complicate efforts by other countries to develop domestic photovoltaic industries. This raises questions about energy security, technological independence and the future of global clean-energy supply chains.
The proposal, announced in October 2026, targets 12 technologies used in solar manufacturing. It also includes processes for producing silicon wafers, advanced solar cells and polysilicon. While some technologies would be prohibited from export, others would be subject to restrictions and additional approval requirements.
The solar industry has benefited from years of falling equipment costs and expanding international trade. The recent proposal by China to control export of solar manufacturing technologies highlights an increasingly important question. Can countries achieve energy independence when the technologies required to manufacture renewable energy equipment remain concentrated in the hands of a few global players?
China’s solar dominance extends beyond finished panels
China is dominating the global solar photovoltaic supply chain. This is supported by extensive manufacturing capacity, investment in research and development, and the development of meshwork industrial networks.
The influence of the second largest economy in the world by GDP also extends beyond the finished solar modules installed on rooftops and utility-scale solar farms. It also features upstream materials, silicon wafers, solar cells and the manufacturing expertise needed to produce these components at scale.
The distinction is important because purchasing solar panels and developing the capacity to manufacture them are two different industrial challenges.
A country can rapidly expand its renewable energy capacity by importing finished modules. Establishing a competitive domestic manufacturing industry, however, requires much more. This will span access to production equipment, specialized engineering knowledge, intellectual property, skilled workers and reliable supply chains.
China’s proposed controls therefore raise concerns that countries seeking to reduce their dependence on imported solar equipment could encounter additional barriers when attempting to acquire the technology needed to manufacture their own products.
According to Reuters’ report on the proposed controls, the measures form part of a broader review of export restrictions. It also covers advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI) and biotechnology.
Beijing has also cited national security concerns. It argues that closer oversight is necessary as photovoltaic (PV) technologies find applications in sensitive sectors, including aerospace and defense.
Importantly, the proposal does not amount to a blanket ban on solar technology exports. Instead, it seeks to spell out technologies that would be prohibited from export and those that could be transferred overseas subject to restrictions.
The industrial implications could extend far beyond China
One of the most significant potential consequences is the effect on countries investing in domestic solar manufacturing.
The United States, India and European economies are set to face major blows. China’s export controls on solar manufacturing technologies has the potential to affect the economies’ plans to expand domestic clean-energy manufacturing. These challenges are also particularly relevant to Africa, where countries are expanding solar deployment while exploring opportunities to develop domestic manufacturing capabilities. China’s proposed controls could also affect Africa’s solar manufacturing ambitions.
This is so because, building factories is only part of the equation. Manufacturers must also obtain the technology and expertise required to operate production lines efficiently. They also need to remain competitive as solar technology evolves.
Restrictions on advanced manufacturing know-how could complicate those efforts. Particularly, where companies depend on Chinese processes, equipment or technical assistance.
The proposed measures could also affect the international expansion strategies of manufacturers seeking to establish production facilities outside China. Technology transfers, licensing agreements and the installation or commissioning of manufacturing lines could become more complicated where controlled technologies are involved.
This could increase compliance costs, delay projects or encourage manufacturers to seek alternative suppliers and develop their own processes.
The proposal also highlights the vulnerability of countries attempting to develop manufacturing capacity in emerging technologies. Advanced processes such as perovskite-silicon tandem cells offer the potential for improved solar conversion efficiency. Access to such processes is becoming increasingly important as the solar manufacturing industry moves beyond conventional production methods.
If access to some of these technologies becomes more restricted, competing manufacturers could find it harder to close the technological gap.
Could China’s solar export controls move accelerate the search for alternatives?
China’s proposed restrictions could also create additional incentives for countries to invest in domestic research and development. The export controls could also catalyze the establishment of alternative technology partnerships and the diversification of sources of manufacturing equipment.
India, for example, has been seeking to reduce its reliance on Chinese solar technology. Restrictions affecting technology transfers could make that objective more difficult in the short term, but they could also strengthen the case for investing in independent manufacturing capabilities.
Other countries could pursue similar strategies. Also noteworthy is that developing competitive production processes requires considerable capital, technical expertise and time.
There is also a risk that increasingly fragmented technology markets could undermine some of the efficiencies that have helped drive down solar costs. If manufacturers must develop parallel production systems or source technologies from a narrower range of suppliers, the industry could face higher costs and slower deployment of advanced manufacturing methods.
Conversely, stronger investment in alternative technologies could eventually produce a more diversified global supply chain.
Whether that outcome materializes will depend on the willingness of governments and private investors to support manufacturing beyond the initial construction of factories.
Energy security now includes control over manufacturing technology
The proposed export controls on solar manufacturing technologies by China also illustrates how energy security is evolving.
Historically, many governments focused on securing fuel supplies, electricity generation capacity and access to critical raw materials. As renewable energy becomes increasingly important, the ability to manufacture the equipment that generates and distributes electricity is also becoming a political and strategic concern.
Solar power reduces exposure to imported fossil fuels. Dependence can also shift elsewhere in the supply chain if countries rely heavily on foreign suppliers for panels, components and manufacturing technology.
This does not mean that every country needs to manufacture its own solar equipment. International trade and specialized production remain important sources of affordability and efficiency.
However, governments must weigh the benefits of inexpensive imports against the risks of concentrated supply chains. This is importantly particular to where access to advanced technology could become subject to geopolitical tensions.
China’s proposed solar technology export controls: What happens next?
China’s proposal for solar manufacturing technology export controls is open for public consultation until November 15, 2026.
Until then, it would be premature to conclude overseas solar manufacturing projects will face disruption or that the price of finished solar panels will necessarily rise. Nevertheless, the proposal by China to control export on solar manufacturing technologies is significant.
The global energy transition has largely been driven by the pursuit of cheaper, cleaner electricity. Its next phase could increasingly be shaped by a different contest. Who controls the technologies needed to manufacture the equipment on which that transition depends?

articles.title: China's Solar Exports Keep Falling as Beijing Mulls Export Controls - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.summary: China's Solar Exports Keep Falling as Beijing Mulls Export Controls  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.full_text:
Chinese exports of solar power equipment extended their declining trend this year with a 6.4% drop in September from a year earlier, while China’s authorities consider export controls and/or bans on a dozen solar manufacturing technologies.
The world’s top solar manufacturer shipped 1.21 million metric tons of solar cells and panels last month, according to customs data cited by Reuters.
While the exports rose from August, they were over 6% lower compared to September last year, and contributed to a year-to-date slump of 9.5% in overseas solar equipment shipments.
China’s exports of solar cells and panels began to drop in May after Beijing removed the local export tax rebate as of April 1, which depressed export volumes. The world’s top solar panel and cell manufacturer scrapped, effective April 1, 2026, export tax rebates for the value-added tax (VAT) of photovoltaic products, including solar cells and panels. China will also withdraw the export tax rebate on battery products, effective January 1, 2027. The Chinese tax policy change was widely expected to slow solar exports from April 2026 onwards, as the policy raises export costs and makes Chinese PV products more expensive internationally.
China is now proposing a trade policy that could limit its exports of some solar technologies, including those for manufacturing high-efficiency solar products such as perovskite, tandem solar, polysilicon, wafer, and crystalline-silicon cell production tech.
The proposed changes are part of a wider effort to limit exports of as many as 40 technologies in the artificial intelligence, biomedicine, and solar industries to “safeguard national security, protect core technologies and uphold international trade rules.”
The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology last week launched a one-month consultation period for public opinion on the proposed adjustments to China’s catalog of technologies that are subject to export bans or restrictions.
By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

articles.title: Faster services imports threaten to erode cushion against India’s goods trade deficit: Report - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Faster services imports threaten to erode cushion against India’s goods trade deficit: Report  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The emerging concern is that faster growth in services imports could reduce the net foreign exchange earnings generated by India's services sector, weakening an important cushion against the country's large merchandise trade deficit.
Also Read: Christmas cheer, but caution remains: Exporters welcome US tariff relief, keep diversification plans
According to the bank's research report, net services exports declined 10 per cent year-on-year to USD 16.9 billion in September 2026.
The report stated that "net services exports saw a much sharper decline of 10% YoY to USD 16.9bn."
However, when services imports grow faster than exports, the resulting surplus narrows, reducing the amount available to offset the merchandise trade gap.
The trend assumes significance even as India's merchandise exports registered strong growth of 23 per cent year-on-year in September, highlighting differing trends in the country's goods and services trade performance.
Also Read: India needs to leverage FTAs, export promotion mission initiatives to boost shipments: CII's Budhia
However, the September decline does not yet suggest a sustained weakening of India's services trade position.
According to ICICI Bank, cumulative net services exports increased 4 per cent year-on-year to USD 103 billion during April-September 2026, compared with an average monthly surplus of USD 17.1 billion in the first half of FY27 against USD 16.5 billion a year earlier.
The contrasting monthly and half-year trends indicate that while the services sector continues to provide substantial support to India's external trade position, sustaining that cushion will depend on export earnings keeping pace with the country's growing services import bill.
The September figures remain provisional, with subsequent data releases expected to provide greater clarity on whether the slowdown is temporary or reflects a broader moderation in services trade.

articles.title: China’s economy grows faster than forecast after AI boom boosts exports
articles.summary: Third-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demandRoaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending.China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%. Continue readi...
articles.full_text:
Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending.
China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%.
China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures.
Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%.
Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful.
“Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said.
“Hi-tech manufacturing output continues to outperform traditional sectors, as China climbs the value-added ladder,” Wrigley added.
However, fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% over the first nine months, property investment tumbled by 20.6%, and infrastructure spending remained weak.
Data last week showed that China’s exports surged by more than a third in September, lifted by a rise in shipments of electronics related to AI.
“This pickup in GDP growth mainly reflects ongoing export strength on the global AI/tech boom, more than offsetting drags from the Iran conflict and ongoing weakness in domestic demand,” said analysts at ABN Amro.

articles.title: We must tax the wealth of billionaires, not just income. California can lead the way | Ro Khanna
articles.summary: Will California stand with the working class or the oligarchs in the vote this November?The Democratic party has a choice to make. Are we going to be New Deal Democrats or corporate Democrats? Are we standing with the working class or the tech oligarchs?Proposition 40, California’s billionaire tax, is the most important ballot initiative in America and a fight for the soul of our party.Rohit Khanna is aUS congressman and attorney serving as the US representative from California’s 17th congressio...
articles.full_text:
The Democratic party has a choice to make. Are we going to be New Deal Democrats or corporate Democrats? Are we standing with the working class or the tech oligarchs?
Proposition 40, California’s billionaire tax, is the most important ballot initiative in America and a fight for the soul of our party.
Senator Bernie Sanders and I stand with the nurses and healthcare workers who put Prop 40 on the ballot. Governor Gavin Newsom stands with Peter Thiel, Sergey Brin and Elon Musk, Trump backers who all oppose it.
Prop 40 is a one-time 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state. Together they hold wealth equal to half of California’s economy. That wealth is up 20% this year alone.
If they paid this tax, they would be worth the same as they were on Labor Day of this year. That’s the speed at which their wealth is growing. The tax would raise about $100bn, 90% of it for healthcare. It would help keep 3 million Californians from losing coverage. Trump’s cuts could cost Medi-Cal more than $30bn a year, and this tax would help fill that gigantic hole.
Thiel, Brin and Musk have all funded Trump and his party. Thiel gave $1.25m to elect Trump in 2016. Brin gave nearly $500,000 to the Republican National Committee last year. Musk spent roughly $290m to help return Trump to power. On 8 October, Trump awarded Brin and Musk the National Medal of Science.
Brin has spent $102m to kill Prop 40. Thiel gave $3m to block it. Musk attacked it on X, warning that “they will eventually apply the ‘wealth tax’ to everyone”. The day after Trump’s ceremony, Newsom endorsed Prop 42, Brin’s measure to cancel it.
Billionaires have outspent Prop 40’s supporters more than five to one. Musk has given $366n to federal campaigns in this election cycle alone.
Tax billionaires so they can’t buy democracy.
I have made my choice. I endorsed Prop 40, and I will vote no on Prop 42. The California Democratic party took the same positions in August. The governor has made the opposite choice on both.
He fought to keep Prop 40 off the ballot. When the healthcare workers behind it offered to cut the rate to 2% if he would back it, he said no. Now the No on 40 campaign features him in its ads.
Most cynically, Newsom has become the poster child for Prop 42, a billionaire-written provision, which would ban California from ever taxing billionaire wealth.
He will sadly be more remembered for trying to tank Prop 40 (taxing billionaires) than helping pass Prop 50 (redistricting).
Bernie and I believe the fight doesn’t stop with Prop 40. In March, we introduced the Make Billionaires Pay Their Fair Share Act, a 5% annual tax on America’s 938 billionaires, worth $8.2tn.
It would raise more than $4tn over a decade, enough to reverse Trump’s $1.1tn in healthcare cuts, send $12,000 to every family of four making $150,000 or less, and fund free childcare and free college.
I am with the working class.
In 1911, Wisconsin pioneered the income tax because a property tax on land was no longer enough once industry was producing most of the wealth. Two years later, the country adopted the 16th amendment.
Today, California is pioneering a billionaire tax for an economy where explosive asset appreciation escapes ordinary taxation. If voters pass Prop 40, California will be the first place to figure out how to tax billionaire wealth, setting a model for the nation and the world.
For too long, our party has answered to corporate donors before workers. The factory towns and rural counties our governing class ignored stopped believing us. Trump promised to fight for them, then cut taxes for billionaires and cut Medicaid. We will not win those voters back by protecting the same billionaires in Sacramento. You cannot oppose the Trump administration while doing the bidding of its donors.
Anyone who wants to lead this party has to say where they stand on Prop 40.
Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay. In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened.
Will California this November stand with the working class or the oligarchs?
- Rohit Khanna is aUS congressman and attorney serving as the US representative from California’s 17th congressional district

articles.title: Christiane Amanpour announces she’s leaving CNN after 43 years
articles.summary: Anchor’s departure not thought to be linked to company’s recent acquisition by David Ellison’s Skydance MediaChristiane Amanpour, one of CNN’s most decorated and venerated journalists, is leaving the network after 43 years, she said in a statement on Monday.Amanpour, who began working for the then-fledging network as an assistant on the international assignment desk in 1983 and is now its chief international anchor, will end her show Amanpour in May and leave the network at the end of June. She ...
articles.full_text:
Christiane Amanpour, one of CNN’s most decorated and venerated journalists, is leaving the network after 43 years, she said in a statement on Monday.
Amanpour, who began working for the then-fledging network as an assistant on the international assignment desk in 1983 and is now its chief international anchor, will end her show Amanpour in May and leave the network at the end of June. She also hosts a show for PBS, Amanpour and Company, that will conclude at the end of this year.
In the statement, Amanpour said she came to the decision to “separate” from the network “after many months of thought and a few sleepless nights”.
“From my very first big exciting assignment covering the first Gulf war, to the horrors of the Bosnian war, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor,” she wrote.
She ended her statement by encouraging her CNN colleagues: “Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”
Amanpour, 68, has been open about her ongoing treatment for ovarian cancer, which she was diagnosed with in 2021.
Her decision comes at a notable time for the network, which is now part of a larger media conglomerate called Skydance that is run by David Ellison, with heavy backing from Larry Ellison, his Trump-donor father and Oracle co-founder.
Her exit is not thought to be specifically tied to the network’s new ownership, which is viewed skeptically by some CNN journalists because of its perceived closeness to the Trump administration. But, in her statement, Amanpour seemed to nod to concerns about the network’s future, saying that she “will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism”.
She expanded on that commitment to independence in a taped message to viewers of her CNN International show on Monday afternoon.
“You know that I’ve always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you for as long as I am here and beyond,” she said. “That’s especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides – political, financial, and also from the rising dangers in the field.”
In his own memo, CNN’s CEO, Mark Thompson, who announced earlier this month that he will be remaining with the merged company, thanked Amanpour “for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship”.
“Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” Thompson wrote. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.”
Amanpour said she will continue hosting her podcast, The Ex Files and that she “[looks] forward to interesting new projects down the line”.

articles.title: France hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors
articles.summary: Difference between French and German borrowing costs widens after public buildings burned and shops lootedFrance has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country.The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country.
The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt.
The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds rose by as much as 16 basis points to 4.94% on Monday. Yields rise when prices fall, and the bond market sell-off pushed France’s borrowing costs close to a 24-year high.
This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – towards its highest level in 14 years.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs said European sovereign risk was back in focus, with fiscal concerns about France raising the question of whether there could be a repeat of the eurozone debt crisis of 15 years ago.
“The risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion look notably lower. But the fundamental fiscal challenges for some countries – especially in France – look harder now than in 2011-15,” the investment bank said.
“The issue of how to deal with fundamental sovereign risk remains unresolved in the euro area, requiring credible fiscal consolidation.”
The two-year French bond yield rose by nine basis points to 3.64%.
Concerns about France’s instability knocked the euro down to a 17-month low against the pound on Monday morning, when sterling rose to €1.188.
Violence erupted across France after weeks of relatively peaceful demonstrations over conditions in schools and the cost of living, prompting the French president, Emmanuel Macron, to condemn the “unbridled violence” in a televised address on Sunday night.
Tens of thousands of people have attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups have clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.
Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the protests “won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs”, referring to French government bonds.
“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets,” he said.
The 30-year bond, which is a benchmark for the French government’s long-term cost of borrowing, rose by ten basis points to 5.46%.
The rises will put further strain on France’s public finances as the government tries to pass a budget for next year to rein in its deficit.
France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% respectively for the UK.
The unrest adds to “concerns about the political and fiscal troubles in France”, said Neil Wilson, Saxo UK’s investor strategist.
“It underscores how hard it will be for a government to enact the kind of spending restraint required to get the deficit down.”
The French government is preparing a budget that would involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. There are growing fears, however, that political pressure could derail the plans, which could push up borrowing further and add more to the country’s debt pile.
The euro also slipped against the US dollar, down by 0.4% at one stage on Monday to $1.1197.
France’s Cac 40 index, which tracks the biggest companies listed in Paris, fell by 1.4% , compared with a 1.1% drop on the pan-European Stoxx 600 index.
French bank stocks were among the fallers, with Société Générale and BNP Paribas down more than 3%.
Other European stock markets also weakened, with Italy’s FTSE Mib down 1.6% and Spain’s Ibex dropping by 1.9%.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said investors were concerned that higher borrowing costs would increase France’s debt-servicing expenses, reducing its fiscal flexibility at a time when growth is already subdued.
“But France is not alone,” he said. “Spain faces its own political constraints around budgets and fiscal reforms, although stronger economic growth provides some protection, while Italy’s substantial debt stock leaves it particularly sensitive to prolonged periods of elevated yields.”

articles.title: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’
articles.summary: The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listingAnthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing.The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every ...
articles.full_text:
Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing.
The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every 50% increase in its value above an undisclosed baseline.
The fund will allow Anthropic to “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”, the company said.
The move comes amid growing public nervousness about AI, from the threat to human labour to the impact on the environment and its influence on social behaviours.
“AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic wrote in a blogpost.
It said that while it had already committed $200m to addressing the issue, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”
The company, which is preparing to list on the stock market, has called for a slowdown in breakneck development of AI, a warning later echoed by rivals such as OpenAI.
Anthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round. The company is reportedly considering a $1.5tn valuation when it floats on the stock market, with an IPO planned for November.
Last week, Anthropic said some of its AI models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners.
It said that once this happens, the models would be able to power themselves without the need of datacentres.
Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and founder of SpaceX, responded to Anthropic’s plans for a public benefit fund on social media by pledging to give some of his own shares away.
“I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” he wrote. “This is what I will be doing.”
He later announced: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.”
Shares in SpaceX, which is listed on the Nasdaq in the US, rose by 1% in pre-market trading on Monday. The company has lost about 9% of its value since it joined the stock market in June.
OpenAI, the developer behind ChatGPT, also reportedly engaged in early talks to give a 5% stake in its organisation to the US government.
Anthropic, which was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, was established as a public benefit corporation. It means that all of the company’s directors must balance financial returns with its public interest mission.
